entries.text: On Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen the score arrived fully separated, out to 60 channels, with orchestral elements split and percussion divided into high, mid and low, so Summers could remove elements where clarity demanded.

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

entries.text: Summers found that heavy percussion under robot running-and-shooting sequences tends to become a cacophony. In other scenes the director chose to let the music drive, and the effects came down instead.

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

entries.text: Summers mixed against the composer team's high-quality orchestral mock-ups early, learning where the score was thick and where effects could embellish it. When the real cue arrived, it only brought more clarity and transparency.

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

entries.text: Some cues were written for scenes where the director wasn't sure he needed music. Once they sat with the dialogue, Summers found some scenes carried themselves without the cue, while others fell flat without music.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: In Alice in Wonderland, London was kept deliberately bland and 'normal', while Underland got exotic birds, insects and frogs layered for depth. Each location had its own sound: a lush castle by waterfalls versus a battlefield with only stark, lonely wind.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: For Alice's 3D version Johnson pushed elements, even dialogue, into the surrounds and panned dialogue to the speaker's position in frame. The same moves proved distracting in 2D, which got much less dialogue panning.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: When Alice changes size, her voice quality was left untouched so it wouldn't distract from the performance. Instead the room reverb tightened when she was big and grew larger and more alive when she was small, and her big footsteps got deeper.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: Johnson felt Alice's size-change visuals were so strong that equally bold sound would diminish their impact, so the visuals told most of it. Backgrounds still helped: when she was small, grass became important because the blades were as big as her.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: On The Hot Spot, an early mix Johnson did with Gary Rydstrom, Dennis Hopper's first note was that the dialogue 'sounds kinda weird.' After replaying the scene, Hopper decided it simply sounded much cleaner than he was used to.

source.title: "Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: The pod race had no music or dialogue to pace it, so the mixers varied effects intensity and volume. The announcer justified pulling the race back; returning to the pods at lower intensity than before left room to build as the race progressed.

entries.text: Instead of filling the track with distant footsteps and background chatter for thick ambiences, as many sci-fi films did, The Phantom Menace's mixers aimed for a more discreet sound so audiences felt an intimate part of the experience.

entries.text: Hymns treats Pro Tools as just another tool, like Moviola or Steenbeck. For him good taste means three things: selecting sounds, synchronizing them to picture, and knowing when to pay extreme attention to detail versus being lighter and broader.

source.title: Robert Redford's Golden Ears: The Sound Editors of 'Lions for Lambs'

entries.text: Across five Robert Redford films, Hymns noticed an evocative, sad sense of loss that isn't there on first viewing but arrives during post. On each film he tries to pinpoint where and why it comes in.

source.title: Robert Redford's Golden Ears: The Sound Editors of 'Lions for Lambs'

entries.text: For Blue Velvet's slap, Hymns cut slaps, a ruler on a desk, a huge pumpkin struck by hands and a steel rule, and a dozen slaps on an assistant's bare shoulder. Alan Splet picked takes and mixed every layer together.

source.title: Efeitos industriais, detalhes artesanais: entrevista com o editor de som Richard Hymns

entries.text: For The Mosquito Coast, Splet gave Hymns 250 explosions to audition, choosing the best short, medium and long-range one for each blast. He also had Hymns cut the last two and a half frames before each explosion to zero, intensifying the impact.

source.title: Efeitos industriais, detalhes artesanais: entrevista com o editor de som Richard Hymns

entries.text: Hymns says that if audiences leave raving about how impressive the sound was, he has somewhat failed. He wants them to believe that's how war sounded in Saving Private Ryan, or how the dinosaurs sounded on set.

source.title: Efeitos industriais, detalhes artesanais: entrevista com o editor de som Richard Hymns

entries.text: For a period Volvo in Bridge of Spies, Hymns found 1964 Nagra recordings of the same car, then brand-new, in the British Cinesound library Peter Jackson had bought. Every time the Volvo is heard, it's that vintage recording.

source.title: Efeitos industriais, detalhes artesanais: entrevista com o editor de som Richard Hymns

entries.text: For an axe attack in Warning Sign, Splet replaced the office door with a bolted two-panel wooden door, put contact mics inside and outside, and had Hymns and a colleague chop it apart, rather than using a library axe.

source.title: Efeitos industriais, detalhes artesanais: entrevista com o editor de som Richard Hymns

entries.text: Winds and fires are hard sounds, Hymns says: they can turn into white noise, into nothing, and end up all sounding alike. He credits Alan Splet with making them sound genuinely sophisticated.

entries.text: A clean ambience takes three things, Boyes says: a location with a beautiful natural ambience, a time free of motors on the ground and planes overhead, and superb equipment. In Costa Rica he recorded every time of day and night.

source.title: Sound Effects Recording, April 1997

entries.text: In dense jungle, Boyes prefers recording one location from two or three perspectives over a single 360-degree capture, since turning a slightly directional mic 180 degrees changes the sound entirely. He then mixes the perspectives as he likes.

entries.text: In The Lord of the Rings, some scenes let music carry events at a detached distance, with effects turned ghostly and echoey, weaving through the score. It lifted audiences out of battle intensity and gave them a sonic rest.

entries.text: Editorial wanted the Uruk-hai march on Helm's Deep huge; Peter Jackson asked for subtle: feel the pulse but hear the waiting warriors breathe. Since the scene descends into chaos, starting quiet gave the mix something to build with.

entries.text: For Avatar's big explosions, Boyes built the percussive attack by truncating the transient elements of favorite explosions on the Synclavier keyboard, playing them as a sharp attack with a quick decay, followed by a sonic wash.

source.title: Avatar

entries.text: For Avatar's 3D mix, the team chose only specific elements, like a passing bullet or an arrow, to move back to front, logging frame counts and performing pans frame by frame. Too much sonic information at once would detract.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: Semanick listens for a voice's characteristics and features them. Pushing dialogue above normal conversational level exposes frequencies that don't sound like the person in the room, so he EQs to warm them, and watches shouted lines, which go higher and harder.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: Semanick establishes a room's reverb, then pulls it off as the camera tracks in or characters speak intimately. Pulling reverb and backgrounds down and out, rather than keeping everything up, draws the audience into the characters.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: In Incredibles 2's newscast that follows the signal down the wire, the voice passed through different futzes for the broadcast booth, added static over radio waves, and room reverb that filled then narrowed as the camera moved, with splits on everything.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: Semanick still prefers hardware Lexicon 960 and TC6000 reverbs over their plug-ins, and often futzes through an analog Lafont box. When he A/Bs futz settings, he says directors almost always pick the analog one.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: Directors like David Fincher leave some picture transitions to the mix, expecting sound to fix a clunky cut. Semanick's crossfades and sonic smoothing can help the picture edit tremendously.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: For Mrs. Potato Head's ghostly far-eye voice, Semanick copied her line, advanced it several frames, sent it to reverb, printed only the reverb return and reversed it so it preceded the dialogue. He then added delays and reverb to the original.
